changes.before: An equity committee or unit equity team needs a clear charter to do real work. Learn to charter, staff and steer one with clear decision rights, fair membership, owned actions and accountability that measures systems rather than people.
changes.after: Develop an equity committee with a clear purpose, approved work time and defined authority. Practice sharing responsibilities, coordinating existing efforts and reporting what changes for people served.
changes.reason: Clarify committee authority, approved work capacity, formal referrals, consultation, evidence and accountability.

changes.before:
Equity committees and unit equity teams are common in Minnesota state government, and they are easy to set up badly. A group forms with energy, meets monthly, generates ideas, and a year later members cannot say what changed or who was supposed to act. Most of these problems trace back to an unclear purpose and unclear decision rights, not to the people involved.

Start with context. The governor's first executive order created the One Minnesota Council on Diversity, Inclusion, and Equity, and a later order replaced that first order, renewing the council alongside the Governor's Community Council on Inclusion and Equity. That later order refers to agency-specific equity plans and a statewide long-range plan, with annual reporting to the Governor. Executive orders can be changed by future governors, so check the current order before citing it. Within DHS, the agency's published equity policy has called for equity committees in each administration to advise leadership and for equity analysis of legislative proposals. Your committee sits inside this landscape: it helps the agency carry out commitments that leaders are already accountable for, rather than inventing a parallel mission.

A charter makes the group's role explicit. At minimum it should state the purpose in one or two sentences, the scope (which division, unit or program), membership and terms, how members are selected, meeting time and whether it is paid work time, the executive sponsor, how decisions are made, how the group reports and to whom, and when the charter will be reviewed. It should also state what the group does not do. An equity committee does not investigate complaints, decide accommodations, handle grievances, conduct Tribal consultation or give legal advice. Those belong to the Equal Opportunity and Access Division, Human Resources, labor relations, the ADA coordinator, the Tribal liaison and legal counsel. Knowing when to refer is one of the most valuable things a committee can do.

Decision rights are the heart of the charter. For each kind of work, say whether the group decides, recommends, is consulted or is informed. A unit equity team might decide its own meeting agenda and training topics, recommend changes to a notice template, be consulted on a hiring process redesign and be informed of budget decisions. Writing this down protects members from being blamed for decisions they never controlled and protects leaders from surprise when a recommendation arrives.
changes.after:
An equity committee needs agreement about its work and the decisions its members can make. Without that agreement, useful proposals may remain unanswered while members take on work outside their authority. A charter gives the group and its sponsor a common reference for setting goals, arranging time and resolving questions.

Connect the charter to the agency's duties. Executive Order 23-12 continued the One Minnesota Council and the Governor's Community Council and described support for agency equity plans. It assigned an annual report to the One Minnesota Council, not every local committee. Check the order's current status when applying it. The published DHS Equity Policy gives equity directors and area equity committees roles in putting the policy into practice. It includes committee actions and legislative proposals among the uses of the DHS Equity Analysis Toolkit.

A useful charter states the group's purpose, scope, member selection, terms, sponsor, reporting plan and review date. Describe the work time needed and obtain approval from the people who control that time and budget. The charter records approved plans; it does not by itself authorize pay, overtime, position changes or decisions reserved to another office. For each activity, say whether the group decides, recommends, gives advice or receives information. A team might set an approved meeting agenda while proposing a notice change for the program manager's decision.

Name the formal routes for complaints, accommodations, grievances, legal questions and Tribal consultation. Being a committee member does not give someone authority to investigate conduct or decide these matters. Follow the applicable Human Resources, Equal Opportunity and Access Division, labor relations, ADA, legal or Tribal liaison process. Sharing a contact is useful, but members must also meet their own reporting duties. Under MMB Policy 1436, managers and supervisors must immediately report protected-class harassment or discrimination allegations to Human Resources or the affirmative action officer. DHS policy also requires prompt referral to Equal Opportunity and Access. Address urgent protection needs through the responsible office without waiting for a committee meeting or charter review.
changes.reason: Clarify committee authority, approved work capacity, formal referrals, consultation, evidence and accountability.

changes.before: A clear charter names the purpose, the sponsor, paid time, what the group decides versus recommends, and what it refers to formal offices. Most committee frustration comes from unclear decision rights.
changes.after: Record the committee’s approved authority, resources and referral paths. A charter does not replace formal reporting duties or grant powers reserved to another office.
changes.reason: Clarify committee authority, approved work capacity, formal referrals, consultation, evidence and accountability.

changes.before:
Researchers in academic medicine coined the phrase minority tax to describe the extra responsibilities placed on faculty from underrepresented groups in the name of diversity efforts. Rodriguez, Campbell and Pololi described how these faculty are often asked to serve on diversity committees and represent their communities, while that work is not recognized in promotion. The setting is different from state government, but the pattern is familiar: the same few colleagues, often staff of color, disabled staff or others with lived experience of exclusion, carry equity work on top of a full workload, and that effort is invisible when it comes time for assignments, reviews or advancement.

A committee that depends on unrecognized labor is not equitable in its own design. Leaders can prevent this in concrete ways. Make committee service paid work time, and say so in the charter. Agree with each member's supervisor on how much time the role takes and what other work will move to make room. Use fixed terms with rotation so the work does not settle on the same people. Recruit broadly, including colleagues who hold positional power and people who are new to the topic, so that the burden of explaining inequity does not fall only on those who experience it. Recognize the work in position descriptions and development plans where appropriate, without turning it into a rating.

Be careful about representation. No member speaks for an entire community, and no one should be expected to disclose their race, disability, faith, immigration history or other identity to join or contribute. Invite people because of their interest, skills and role. When the group needs community perspective, go to the community through proper engagement, advisory bodies or Tribal consultation, rather than asking a staff member to stand in.

Keep structures distinct. Enterprise employee resource groups, coordinated by Minnesota Management and Budget, are employee-led groups with their own bylaws, work plans and executive sponsors, and MMB guidelines state they cannot replace labor-management committees. An agency equity committee is a management-chartered body that advises on programs and operations. Labor-management committees handle issues under collective bargaining agreements. Confusing these can lead to a committee drifting into matters that belong to bargaining or to ERG members being treated as unpaid consultants.
changes.after:
Committee work takes time that otherwise would go to another task. When leaders invite participation without adjusting assignments, members may face conflicting expectations about their regular work and their committee work. Discuss those demands before selecting members, and revisit them when service needs or committee commitments change.

In a 2015 discussion article, Rodriguez, Campbell and Pololi examine the minority tax in academic medicine. They describe unequal diversity duties and work that may receive little credit when faculty seek promotion. The authors discuss a term already in use; they do not claim to have created it. This offers a question for state workplaces: who is repeatedly asked to contribute, and how is that work supported? It does not establish a local pattern by itself or tell you what an individual colleague experiences. Examine assignments and ask about capacity without inferring a person's needs from identity.

Arrange approved work time through a written agreement that names hours, coverage and duties that will change. Seek Human Resources or labor relations guidance where pay, position duties or a labor agreement is involved. Do not rely on a charter alone to authorize those changes. If adequate capacity is unavailable, reduce the scope or obtain a resourced schedule before assigning more work. Recruit beyond the usual volunteers, invite colleagues with relevant authority and use rotating terms where continuity allows. Give the work credit through approved development and recognition plans. This program’s learning activities do not replace formal employee reviews.

No member represents every person who shares an identity or experience. Invite interest, skills and relevant work perspectives without pressuring colleagues to disclose personal histories. That practice does not cancel a separate lawful duty to provide information. When community input is needed, offer accessible ways for people affected to contribute. A staff member’s views cannot replace formal consultation between governments, arranged through the Tribal liaison.

Keep the group's purpose distinct from other structures. MMB's enterprise employee resource groups are employee-led networks with their own rules, including sponsors, bylaws and work plans. Their guidelines bar bargaining over employment terms or handling grievances. They also state that these groups do not replace labor-management committees. An equity committee's authority comes from its approved agency role; it should coordinate with these groups without assuming their functions or treating their members as an unlimited source of labor.
changes.reason: Clarify committee authority, approved work capacity, formal referrals, consultation, evidence and accountability.

changes.before: Design membership so equity work is paid, time-limited, shared and recognized, and never depends on colleagues disclosing identity or speaking for a whole community.
changes.after: Agree on approved time, coverage and a manageable scope before assigning committee work. Share responsibility without treating identity as expertise or expecting one person to represent a community.
changes.reason: Clarify committee authority, approved work capacity, formal referrals, consultation, evidence and accountability.

changes.before:
Before a committee proposes new work, it should know what already exists. In a large agency, equity-related activity is often scattered: a program team running an equity analysis on a policy change, a communications unit testing plain-language notices, a data team disaggregating results, a training cohort, a county partnership, an interpreter access project. An activity inventory lists these in one place with a few fields each: what the activity is, who owns it, which population or process it affects, what change it aims for, its status, and any evidence of results. The inventory is not an audit of anyone's performance. It is a map.

The inventory reveals three things. First, duplication: two units separately building the same resource. Second, gaps: a process with known disparities that no one is working on. Third, orphaned work: good efforts that lost their owner when someone changed jobs. Compare the inventory with the agency's equity plan and division priorities. The State of Minnesota Equity Analysis Toolkit emphasizes defining intended outcomes, the people affected, resources and accountability, and those same headings work well for sorting what you find.

Then write action plans, and keep them short. A committee that adopts twenty actions will finish very few. Choose a small number of actions that are within the group's decision rights or that a named leader has agreed to own. Each action should state the specific change (not the topic), the owner, the partners who must be involved, the resources and time needed, the first milestone, how you will know whether it worked, and when you will review it. The GARE toolkit cautions that implementation must be realistic and adequately resourced; an unfunded action is a wish.

Include the people affected. If an action changes how people receive services, plan how self-advocates, families, county and Tribal staff or community partners will be engaged before the design is fixed, and how you will report back to them. If an action touches Tribal Nations, involve the DHS Tribal liaison and follow the agency's consultation policy; Minnesota law requires DHS and other listed agencies to consult with Tribal governments on matters with Tribal implications. The committee's role is to coordinate and advise, not to substitute for that government-to-government relationship.
changes.after:
Before proposing new work, identify relevant activity already underway in the division or unit. A DSD policy team might be reviewing guidance while a communications team tests notice wording and a data team examines response patterns. Record each activity's owner, focus, intended change, current status and available evidence. Use information the committee is authorized to access, and keep individual case or personnel details out of a general coordination inventory.

An inventory can suggest overlapping work, unmet needs and efforts whose ownership is uncertain. It does not prove duplication: two teams may serve different populations or have separate requirements. Confirm what you find with the responsible owners before recommending a change. Compare the work with agency priorities and the state Equity Analysis Toolkit's questions about intended results, engagement, evidence and accountability. Describe missing information so readers can distinguish a verified gap from an unanswered question.

Choose commitments that match the group's authority and available resources. A long list may be useful as a record of suggestions, but it is not a promise to implement everything. For each proposed action, name the specific change, accountable owner, partners, required time and resources, first milestone, measure and review date. Obtain the responsible leader's agreement before assigning their team work. If resources are uncertain, record that dependency and the decision needed rather than presenting the action as funded. Keep other suggestions visible and explain how priorities were selected.

Plan accessible engagement while participants can still influence the design. A service notice change might require perspectives from people receiving services, county partners, interpreters and disability advocates. Explain how feedback will be considered and report back in a form participants can use. Coordinate data collection and sharing with the responsible privacy and records staff rather than assuming consent permits every use.

Where a proposal may have Tribal implications, involve the DHS Tribal liaison early and follow the agency's consultation process. Minnesota Statutes section 10.65 requires timely, meaningful consultation with the affected Tribal governments and consideration of that input in agency decisions. General outreach, an advisory meeting or a staff member's contribution does not fulfill that formal relationship. The committee can identify the need and support coordination while authorized officials carry out consultation.
changes.reason: Clarify committee authority, approved work capacity, formal referrals, consultation, evidence and accountability.

changes.before: Stopping owned work to centralize control wastes progress. The committee's role is to coordinate and connect, not to take over.
changes.after: The committee has no stated authority to stop those teams’ work. Confirm overlap with the owners and coordinate recommendations through the responsible leaders before proposing a change.
changes.reason: Clarify committee authority, approved work capacity, formal referrals, consultation, evidence and accountability.

changes.before: Start an activity inventory for your unit or division using the fields in the job aid. Aim for at least five entries this week, and note one duplication, one gap or one orphaned effort to raise with your committee or sponsor.
changes.after: Start an inventory using authorized information and the job aid fields. Identify several current activities, then confirm one possible overlap, unmet need or ownership question with the responsible people before raising a recommendation.

changes.before:
Accountability for equity work should fall on commitments and systems, not on scoring individual people. This program does not rank staff, and committees should not build tools that do. Measures that tally which employees completed the most equity activities, or that rate units against each other in a public list, tend to reward appearance over change, invite gaming and can expose staff who already carry more of this work. They also shift attention away from the question that matters: did the process get better for the people it serves?

Useful measures fall into three types. Process measures show whether the committed work happened: the share of policy proposals that received an equity analysis before submission, or whether notice templates were tested with readers. Outcome measures show whether the process performs better: time to arrange an interpreter, the rate at which people respond to a notice by the deadline, or the gap in approval rates for a service across groups, where data quality supports it. Experience measures come from the people affected, gathered with consent and without requiring identity disclosure. For each measure, state the source, the baseline, how often you will look and who will interpret it. Report the limits of your data along with the results.

The executive sponsor is the committee's link to authority. A good sponsor attends often enough to understand the work, carries recommendations to the leadership table, secures time and resources, removes barriers, and tells the committee plainly when a recommendation is declined and why. A sponsor is not the committee's supervisor, spokesperson in every setting or a substitute for formal offices. Agree on how the committee will bring decisions to the sponsor: a short written recommendation stating the change, the evidence, the options considered, the owner proposed and the decision needed by a date.

When a decision stalls, escalate respectfully and in writing. Remind the sponsor of the decision needed and its effect on people served. If the matter belongs elsewhere, such as a legislative proposal, a contract change or a statewide policy, ask the sponsor to route it. At least once a year, report what changed, what did not and why, both to leadership and to the staff and community partners who contributed. Honest reporting about slow progress builds more trust than a polished summary.
changes.after:
A committee needs evidence about the commitments it made and the effect of its work. Attendance can show participation, but it cannot establish that service access improved. For this program, use measures of processes and results rather than creating personal equity scores or competitive participation rankings. This learning approach does not replace required training records, authorized workforce evaluation or other official reporting responsibilities.

Process measures describe whether an agreed action occurred, such as testing revised notices with readers before release. Outcome measures describe results, such as the share of notices receiving a response by the deadline. Those results may improve, remain unchanged or worsen, and a change alone does not establish its cause. Experience measures add what people affected report about using the process. Consider these sources together instead of treating one favorable number as proof of success.

For each measure, record its source, baseline, population, time period, review frequency and responsible interpreter. Explain the denominator behind a rate, missing information and other changes that could affect comparison. Disaggregate results only through authorized data practices, and protect small groups from identification. When seeking feedback, explain its purpose, use and privacy limits, with participation choices appropriate to that process. Consent alone does not authorize otherwise restricted collection, access or disclosure.

The sponsor connects recommendations to the people authorized to decide and resource them. Agree on how the sponsor receives proposals, responds to unresolved decisions and explains a declined recommendation. A sponsor may also hold a supervisory role, but those responsibilities should remain clear rather than being assumed from the sponsor title. The role does not replace Human Resources, Equal Opportunity and Access, legal counsel or other designated offices.

When a decision stalls, provide a brief written account of the requested change, evidence, options, proposed owner and date needed. Explain the practical effect of delay and ask the sponsor to route matters beyond the committee's authority. Urgent reporting or protection duties continue through their formal channels. Set a reporting schedule in the charter; an annual account can be useful, but it is a program recommendation unless an applicable policy requires it. Report what happened, what remains uncertain and what decision comes next, using information approved for the intended audience.
changes.reason: Clarify committee authority, approved work capacity, formal referrals, consultation, evidence and accountability.
